Choices.A: On a profit-volume chart, the vertical intercept equals negative fixed costs, the slope equals the contribution margin ratio, and breakeven sits where the line crosses zero
Choices.B: The slope of the profit-volume line equals the gross-margin ratio
Choices.C: The line begins at the breakeven point on the vertical axis
Choices.D: A flatter slope produces more profit at any given volume level

CommonTrapReference: Confusing the profit-volume slope with gross margin instead of contribution margin.
ExplanationCorrect: At zero volume the firm loses exactly its fixed costs, so the line intercepts the vertical axis at minus fixed costs. Every unit sold adds its CONTRIBUTION margin to profit, so the slope is the CM ratio - steeper wherever variable costs are thinner relative to price. Profit crosses zero precisely at breakeven volume. The chart compresses CVP into one picture: read the intercept for risk, the slope for operating leverage, and the crossover for safety margin.
ExplanationWrongB: Gross margin deducts only production cost of sales; the PV line responds to ALL variable costs including selling and administrative ones. Slope equals the CM ratio - that substitution is what makes the chart a decision tool rather than a reporting artifact.
ExplanationWrongC: The line starts at MINUS fixed costs when volume is zero - losses come first, breakeven arrives only where the rising line crosses the axis. Starting at breakeven describes nothing on a profit-volume chart.
ExplanationWrongD: Flatter means LESS contribution per dollar of sales: at any volume above breakeven a flatter line sits LOWER on the profit axis. Slope steepness and profit generation move together, never inversely.
Stem: A new analyst receives Riverbend Outfitters' profit-volume chart and must interpret its geometry. Which reading is correct?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: Intercept = -FC; slope = CM ratio; zero-crossing = breakeven

Choices.A: Shut down immediately because price sits below average total cost
Choices.B: Continue in the short run - price covers variable cost with $6 toward fixed costs - but plan restructuring or exit if the economics persist below full cost over the long run
Choices.C: Expand aggressively because variable costs are comfortably covered
Choices.D: Continue at any cost structure indefinitely, since revenue exceeds some measure of cost

CommonTrapReference: Applying the short-run shutdown test when the question is really about long-run viability.
ExplanationCorrect: Two horizons impose two tests. SHORT RUN: operate while price covers AVC - each unit contributes $6 ($28 - $22) toward unavoidable fixed costs, making operation strictly better than shutting down today. LONG RUN: nothing survives below ATC forever; if $28 cannot rise or $30 cannot fall, capacity should exit as assets exhaust. Conflating the horizons produces both classic errors - premature shutdown that converts small losses into total ones, and indefinite persistence that bleeds capital.
ExplanationWrongA: ATC includes fixed costs already committed - shutting down does not recover them, it merely guarantees their full weight becomes loss. The short-run comparison runs against VARIABLE cost alone.
ExplanationWrongC: Covering AVC justifies CONTINUING, never expanding: expansion commits new capital into the same sub-full-cost economics that make exit the long-run question.
ExplanationWrongD: Some measure of cost is doing heroic work in that sentence - revenue exceeding variable cost but not full cost is precisely the zone where continuing today and exiting tomorrow are both correct.
Stem: Brynn Manufacturing's product sells at $28 against variable cost of $22 and full cost of $30, with committed capacity that cannot be redeployed this year. Which course does relevant analysis support?
Topic: C.150 Short-run continue versus long-run exit
VerifiedChecks: Independent: P > AVC continue now (+6/unit); P < ATC exit long-run

Choices.A: Drop the printer line - it loses $20,000 annually after its avoidable costs
Choices.B: Drop the printer line - elimination saves the full $140,000 of avoidable fixed costs
Choices.C: KEEP the printer line - dropping it sacrifices roughly $110,000 of annual contribution: the line net position disappears AND $90K of accessory sales attached to installed printers vanishes
Choices.D: Keep the printer line because allocated corporate costs will disappear with it

CommonTrapReference: Evaluating a product line in isolation, ignoring complementary sales attached to it.
ExplanationCorrect: Standalone view: printer contribution $120,000 less avoidable fixed costs $140,000 = negative $20,000 - a loser. But printers SELL accessories: dropping the line removes $90,000 of ink-and-supply contribution attached to the installed base. Full dropping effect = lose roughly $110K of annual contribution versus keeping. Complementary products invert standalone segment rankings: the printer operates as a customer-acquisition device whose profit shows up in someone else line.
ExplanationWrongA: The standalone loss is real but INCOMPLETE: dropping the line also removes $90K of accessory contribution sold into the installed base. The decision-relevant comparison nets both effects - roughly $110K of annual contribution surrendered versus keeping.
ExplanationWrongB: Avoidable fixed costs are saved only if production actually stops AND no complementary sales go with it. Here elimination costs $110K net - the $140K saving figure treats gross avoidable cost as the decision variable instead of the net effect.
ExplanationWrongD: Allocated corporate costs persist regardless of the printer decision - they are neither saved by dropping nor caused by keeping. Anchoring the recommendation on allocation relief double-counts costs that stay.
Stem: Atlas Fabrication's printer line shows contribution of $120,000 against avoidable fixed costs of $140,000. Dropping printers would also eliminate $90,000 of ink-and-supply contribution sold to the installed base. Should the line be dropped?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: -20K standalone plus 90K accessories lost -> keep

Choices.A: 17,143 units - dividing fixed costs by the premium-tier contribution margin
Choices.B: 24,000 units - dividing fixed costs by the lowest-tier contribution margin
Choices.C: 9,600 units - dividing fixed costs by the variable cost per unit
Choices.D: 20,000 units - blended price of $37 less $25 variable cost gives $12 blended contribution; $240,000 divided by $12

CommonTrapReference: Using one tier price or margin for a mixed-price product line.
ExplanationCorrect: With two price tiers selling in constant proportion, use WEIGHTED values: blended price = 0.70 x $40 + 0.30 x $30 = $37; blended contribution = $37 - $25 = $12. Breakeven = $240,000 / $12 = 20,000 units. Any single-tier shortcut misprices 30-70 percent of the mix and moves the answer by thousands of units.
ExplanationWrongA: That figure divides fixed costs by a $14 margin matching no tier - premium units contribute $15, discount units $5. The blended reality is $12, giving 20,000 rather than 17,143.
ExplanationWrongB: 24,000 prices EVERY unit at the discount tier $10 margin even though 70 percent of volume earns $15 - overstating the requirement by 4,000 units and distorting the launch plan upward.
ExplanationWrongC: Variable cost has NO role in breakeven arithmetic - the denominator must be CONTRIBUTION per unit. Dividing fixed costs by what units COST rather than what they contribute produces a number without meaning.
Stem: Software vendor Selwyn sells in two tiers: 70% of units at $40 and 30% at $30; variable cost is $25 across both tiers; fixed costs run $240,000. What is the breakeven unit volume?

Choices.A: PRIORITIZE Product B - yield-adjusted contribution is $15.00 per constraint-hour versus Product A $9.50, despite A higher unit margin
Choices.B: Prioritize Product A - its $20 unit contribution exceeds B $15
Choices.C: Either priority yields identical throughput value because both products consume the same constraint
Choices.D: Prioritize A using unadjusted hourly figures - $10.00 versus $8.00 per hour

CommonTrapReference: Ranking constrained-resource products by unit margin without adjusting for scrap yield.
ExplanationCorrect: The constraint measures HOURS, so rank by contribution per hour of GOOD output. Product A: 5 percent of units scrap at zero recovery, so each hour yields only 0.475 good-unit equivalents across two hours - 0.475 x $20 = $9.50/hour. Product B: no defects, one hour each, $15.00/hour. Prioritizing A by unit margin wastes nearly a quarter of scarce hours on scrapped work - the defect rate acts like a hidden tax on every constrained minute.
ExplanationWrongB: Unit margin ignores BOTH the resource consumption rate and the scrap rate - the two factors that determine how much contribution an hour of the bottleneck actually produces. Higher unit margin with worse conversion loses here decisively.
ExplanationWrongC: Identical constraint CONSUMPTION does not mean identical value: an hour spent on A yields $9.50 after scrap while the same hour on B yields $15.00. Throughput VALUE differs by more than half.
ExplanationWrongD: Unadjusted hourly figures use UNIT counts rather than GOOD units: A produces 0.95 salable units per hour (not 0.5), so its true hourly figure is $9.50 - not $10.00 - while B stands at $15.00. The unadjusted comparison also inverts the ranking it claims to support.
Stem: On Barlow's constrained line, Product A contributes $20 per unit but 5% of units are scrapped with zero recovery, and each unit consumes 2 constraint-hours. Product B contributes $15 per unit with no defects at 1 hour each. Which product should the scheduler prioritize?
Topic: C.153 Yield-adjusted contribution on the constraint
VerifiedChecks: Independent: A: 0.475 good/hr x $20 = $9.50/hr versus B: $15/hr -> B

Choices.A: Reject - payback exceeds the two-year hurdle used elsewhere in the company
Choices.B: INVEST - annual benefit of 200 freed hours x $50 = $10,000; payback = $30,000 / $10,000 = 3.0 years, within management four-year requirement
Choices.C: Invest - the benefit reaches $5,000 per year from partial-hour capture
Choices.D: Invest - the benefit reaches $20,000 per year from doubled throughput assumptions

CommonTrapReference: Applying an investment hurdle from the wrong context, or mis-scaling the freed-capacity benefit.
ExplanationCorrect: A 10 percent time reduction on 2,000 bottleneck hours frees 200 hours, worth 200 x $50 = $10,000 of additional contribution annually. Payback = $30,000 / $10,000 = 3.0 years - inside the stated four-year requirement, so invest. The evaluation treats freed CONSTRAINT time at full contribution value because those hours convert directly into salable throughput.
ExplanationWrongA: The two-year hurdle belongs to a different investment class; management stated requirement HERE is four years, and 3.0 clears it comfortably. Importing foreign hurdles buries qualifying projects under borrowed conservatism.
ExplanationWrongC: Halving the benefit to $5,000 has no basis in the data - the full 200 freed hours convert at the stated $50 rate. Arbitrary haircuts bury positive-value improvements under invented caution.
ExplanationWrongD: Doubling the benefit assumes the time reduction repeats twice, which the facts do not support. Overstating benefits fails the decision in the opposite direction - through optimism rather than caution.
Stem: Barlow Products can invest $30,000 to cut processing time by 10% on its bottleneck, which runs 2,000 hours annually at $50 of contribution per hour. Management requires payback within four years. Should Barlow invest?

Choices.B: STRATEGY 2 - its equal-weighted average payoff of ($18M + $12M + $2M) / 3 = $10.67M is the highest simple average
Choices.C: Strategy 1 - its Boom payoff anchors the highest possible outcome
Choices.D: All strategies tie once probabilities are assumed equal

CommonTrapReference: Carrying maximax or maximin conclusions into the Laplace framework, which weights all states equally.
ExplanationCorrect: Laplace assumes NO state is more likely than another - equal weights - and selects the highest simple average. Strategy 1: ($25M + $10M - $5M) / 3 = $10.00M. Strategy 2: ($18M + $12M + $2M) / 3 = $10.67M. Strategy 3: ($12M + $8M + $6M) / 3 = $8.67M. Strategy 2 wins at $10.67M - coinciding with minimax regret on this particular table, though the criteria are logically independent. Note how differently the frameworks rank identical payoffs: maximax takes S1, maximin takes S3, Laplace takes S2.
ExplanationWrongA: Maximin selects the best WORST case - S3 $6M floor - answering a pessimist question. Laplace instead weights all states equally, and S3 $8.67M average trails both rivals.
ExplanationWrongC: Anchoring on the best single outcome repeats the maximax error under a new label. Equal weighting still counts the recession cell: S1 negative $5M drags its average down to $10.0M, below S2 $10.67M.
ExplanationWrongD: The averages span $2M between best and worst - no tie exists. Equal probabilities apply to the STATES, not to the resulting averages.
Stem: CEO Michael Torres evaluates three strategies with payoffs ($M): Strategy 1 - Boom $25, Normal $10, Recession minus $5; Strategy 2 - Boom $18, Normal $12, Recession $2; Strategy 3 - Boom $12, Normal $8, Recession $6. Assuming all states are EQUALLY likely, which strategy does the Laplace criterion select?
